Information asymmetry|idea|idea|asymmetric|§16.1, opening explanation|Distinguish unequal knowledge between parties from uncertainty that both sides share.|local:catalog:information-asymmetry|Same unequal-information meaning; preserve reviewed canonical identity.|Asymmetric information

Adverse selection|idea|idea|insurance|§16.2, The Adverse Selection Problem|See how privately known risk changes which people seek insurance and can push low-risk buyers out.|local:catalog:adverse-selection|Same pre-agreement selection mechanism already in the baseline.|

Moral hazard|idea|idea|insurance|§16.2, The Moral Hazard Problem|Trace how protection from losses can change behavior after insurance is in place.|local:catalog:moral-hazard|Same post-agreement incentive mechanism already represented in the baseline.|

Signaling in economics|idea|idea|asymmetric|§16.1, labor-market credentials paragraphs|Use observable credentials or actions to convey information about otherwise hidden qualities.|local:catalog:economic-signaling|Same signaling identity as the prior candidate; retain registered ID.|Signaling

Screening in economics|idea|idea|asymmetric|§16.1, prospective employer screening paragraph|Let a less-informed party investigate or set requirements to learn hidden characteristics before a transaction.|local:catalog:economic-signaling|Screening is initiated by the less-informed party; signaling is initiated by the better-informed party.|Screening

Reputation in markets|idea|idea|asymmetric|§16.1, used-car dealers and repeat-customer paragraphs|Make future business valuable enough that sellers have a reason to preserve buyers' trust.|local:catalog:information-asymmetry|Reputation is a repeated-interaction response to hidden quality, not the information gap itself.|Market reputation

Warranties as quality assurance|facet_or_application|idea|asymmetric|§16.1, Guarantees, Warranties, and Service Contracts|Shift specified repair or replacement obligations to a seller so buyers need not verify every quality claim beforehand.|local:catalog:information-asymmetry|An explicit remedy commitment differs from uncertainty itself and from an informal reputation.|Warranty

Risk pooling|idea|idea|insurance|§16.2, automobile-insurance example|Combine many uncertain individual losses into a shared pool funded by premiums.|Q43183|Pooling is the collective loss-sharing mechanism; insurance is the broader transfer arrangement.|

Actuarially fair insurance|idea|idea|insurance|§16.2, Risk Groups and Actuarial Fairness|Separate a premium equal to expected claims from one that also funds operating expenses and profit.|local:catalog:actuarially-fair-insurance|Same expected-claims pricing benchmark as the reviewed baseline.|

Insurance deductible|facet_or_application|idea|insurance|§16.2, moral-hazard cost-sharing paragraph|Require an initial out-of-pocket loss amount before the insurance coverage begins paying.|Q43183|A threshold cost-sharing clause is distinct from percentage coinsurance and insurance generally.|Deductible

Coinsurance|facet_or_application|idea|insurance|§16.2, moral-hazard cost-sharing paragraph|Split a covered loss by percentages so the insured party retains part of each covered cost.|Q43183|Percentage sharing differs from a fixed deductible threshold or fixed copayment.|

Bond (finance)|topic|idea|bonds|What are bonds?; What are the benefits and risks? |Treat a bond as an issuer's debt promise to pay specified interest and principal, with default still possible.|Q10863671|The nearest bond-named baseline entry is a chemical phi bond; debt securities and interatomic bonding have different meanings.|Bond;Financial bond

Interest-rate risk in bonds|facet_or_application|idea|bonds|What are the benefits and risks of bonds?, Interest rate risk|Understand why an older fixed-rate bond may need a price discount when newly issued bonds offer higher rates.|Q170924|Interest is a borrowing payment; price sensitivity to changing market rates is a separate investment-risk mechanism.|Interest rate risk

Common-value auction|idea|idea|auction|Lecture 24, Chapter 1|Distinguish shared underlying value from bidders' differing information about that value.|Q37654|This auction valuation model is more specific than the general market mechanism.|Common value auction

Private-value auction|idea|idea|auction|Lecture 24, Chapter 1|Model each bidder's value as personal and unaffected by learning others' valuations, an idealized limiting case.|Q37654|Private preferences differ from uncertainty about a common asset value and from markets generally.|Private value auction

Winner's curse|idea|idea|auction|Lecture 24, Chapter 2, coin-jar demonstration|Condition an estimate on winning because the highest bid may reveal an unusually optimistic initial estimate.|local:catalog:information-asymmetry|This selection effect among uncertain bids differs from unequal information generally.|

First-price sealed-bid auction|idea|idea|auction|Lecture 24, Chapter 3|Submit bids privately and let the highest bidder win while paying their own bid.|Q37654|The payment and disclosure rules define a specific allocation mechanism rather than markets generally.|

Second-price sealed-bid auction|idea|idea|auction|Lecture 24, Chapter 3|Award the item to the highest bidder but charge the second-highest submitted bid.|Q37654|The payment rule differs from first-price auctions even though the highest bidder still wins.|Vickrey auction

Ascending open auction|idea|idea|auction|Lecture 24, Chapter 3|Reveal progressively higher offers until only one bidder remains willing to pay the rising price.|Q37654|Open iterative bidding differs from sealed submissions and descending-price formats.|English auction

Organizational design|topic|idea|orgdesign|§10.1, opening definitions|Choose responsibilities and coordination structures that connect individual work to an organization's purposes.|Q43229|The process of arranging an organization is distinct from an organization as a social entity.|

Formal organization|topic|idea|orgdesign|§10.1, formal organization paragraphs|Specify official roles, reporting lines, and responsibilities so work has an explicit coordination structure.|Q646293|The baseline informal organization concerns emergent ties; formal organization concerns officially assigned relationships.|

Informal organization|topic|idea|orgdesign|§10.1, informal organization paragraphs|Trace the emergent personal connections that influence how work actually gets done beyond the organization chart.|Q646293|Same emergent social structure governing work as the preserved baseline.|

Mechanistic organizational structure|idea|idea|orgdesign|§10.1, Mechanistic and Organic Structures|Coordinate work through hierarchy, standardized procedures, and defined roles where consistency is important.|Q43229|A centralized, rule-driven design is one organizational configuration, not the general entity.|Mechanistic organization

Organic organizational structure|idea|idea|orgdesign|§10.1, Mechanistic and Organic Structures|Distribute decisions and rely on adaptive coordination when work and circumstances change quickly.|Q646293|Organic design deliberately grants flexibility; informal organization names emergent ties that can exist within any formal design.|Organic organization

Functional organizational structure|idea|idea|orgstructures|§4.3, functional structure discussion|Group specialists by expertise while recognizing the risk that departmental boundaries hinder coordination.|Q43229|Grouping by function is a specific organizing rule, distinct from the general organization identity.|Functional structure

Divisional organizational structure|idea|idea|orgstructures|§4.3, divisional structure discussion|Place several functions together within product, market, or regional divisions to concentrate accountability locally.|Q43229|Grouping multiple functions around an output or market differs from a purely functional structure.|Divisional structure

Matrix organization|idea|idea|orgstructures|§4.3, matrix structures discussion|Combine functional and project authority, gaining cross-functional coordination while creating potential dual-boss conflicts.|Q43229|Two simultaneous authority dimensions are distinct from a single reporting hierarchy.|Matrix structure

Networked team structure|facet_or_application|idea|orgstructures|§4.3, networked team structures|Coordinate task-focused teams through flexible relationship networks rather than relying primarily on fixed reporting lines.|Q646293|The proposed facet is intentional organization around task networks; the baseline describes informal ties in organizations generally.|

Virtual organization|idea|idea|orgstructures|§4.3, virtual structures and organizations|Coordinate geographically dispersed expertise and outsourced activities through communication technologies, with trust and isolation challenges.|Q646293|Geographic dispersion and technology-mediated organization are distinct from informal interpersonal ties.|

Span of control|idea|idea|orgstructures|§4.3, opening description of narrow spans|Choose how many people report directly to a manager, affecting oversight and the number of hierarchy layers.|Q43229|A supervisory design variable is narrower than the general organization identity.|

Organizational formalization|idea|idea|orgdesign|§10.1, Formalization|Specify roles, responsibilities, and accountability to different degrees instead of leaving all coordination to emergent relationships.|Q43229|Degree of explicit rule definition differs from the mere existence of an organization or formal chart.|Formalization

Principal–agent problem|idea|idea|firm|§6.10, Principal–agent models|Analyze conflicting interests when one party relies on another's behavior or attributes that contracts cannot fully guarantee.|Q25304581|The principal-agent framework identifies parties and incentive conflicts; incomplete contracts describe the missing enforceable terms.|Principal-agent problem;Agency problem

Incomplete contracts|idea|idea|firm|§6.10, Why are contracts incomplete?|Recognize that important behavior may be unmeasurable, unverifiable, unforeseen, or too costly to specify in an enforceable agreement.|Q25304581|Same economic and legal contract-incompleteness meaning as the registered identity.|Incomplete contract

Employment rent|idea|idea|firm|§6.3, employment rents|Measure the value of holding a job above the worker's next-best alternative, making job loss consequential.|Q28161|The surplus from a particular job is a labor-market incentive quantity, not the entire field.|

Efficiency wage|idea|idea|firm|§6.7–§6.8, labor-discipline model and efficiency-wage equilibrium|Pay above the reservation wage when the induced effort and reduced turnover can justify the extra wage cost.|Q186228|An incentive-driven wage choice differs from a legally imposed minimum wage.|

Worker cooperatives|topic|idea|firm|§6.9, cooperative firms|Separate worker ownership and selection of managers from the day-to-day hierarchy that may still coordinate production.|local:authored:000096|Same worker-owned and democratically governed enterprise meaning as the prior control.|Worker cooperative

Patronage-based surplus distribution|facet_or_application|idea|cooperativeidentity|Principle 3, Member Economic Participation|Allocate cooperative surplus in proportion to member transactions rather than only in proportion to invested capital.|Q4539|A distribution rule within cooperatives is distinct from the general cooperative organization.|Patronage dividend

Just-in-time production|idea|idea|toyota|Just-in-Time; The Pull System|Coordinate production and replenishment with downstream demand to shorten lead times and avoid unnecessary stock.|Q43229|A production-coordination method is distinct from organizations generally.|Just in time;JIT

Jidoka|idea|idea|toyota|Jidoka or Autonomation; Roots of Ideas|Stop work when an abnormality appears so defects are addressed without requiring constant human machine-watching.|Q43229|Built-in abnormality response differs from inventory-timing coordination and ordinary automation.|Autonomation

Apple Inc.|topic|named_subject|firm|Unit 6 opening supply-chain case|Examine a historically documented separation of product ownership, component sourcing, and final assembly across firms and countries.|Q89|The company is distinct from the edible fruit sharing the alias Apple; the source explicitly discusses the business.|Apple

Foxconn|topic|named_subject|firm|Unit 6 opening supply-chain case|See how contract assembly fits into a larger value chain whose components and product ownership sit elsewhere.|Q43229|A specific contract manufacturer differs from organizations generally and from its customer Apple.|

L.L.Bean|topic|named_subject|asymmetric|§16.1, mail-order guarantee example|Use the textbook's mail-order case to see how guarantees and reputation can reduce buyers' uncertainty without inspecting goods.|Q43229|The particular retailer is a documented business case, not the generic reputation mechanism.|L. L. Bean

Panic of 1907|topic|named_subject|panic1907|Opening explanation; trust-company run sequence|Trace how runs on institutions outside the main clearing-house support network disrupted wider financial-market liquidity.|Q22687|A specific historical crisis differs from banks generally and from an abstract bank-run mechanism.|

Knickerbocker Trust Company|topic|named_subject|panic1907|October 18–22 sequence|Examine how uncertain solvency, lost clearing support, and deposit withdrawals culminated in a trust company's suspension.|Q22687|A named institution's documented failure path is distinct from banking generally and the whole 1907 crisis.|

New York Clearing House|topic|named_subject|panic1907|Member support; October 26 loan certificates|See how membership-based mutual liquidity support helped some banks while initially excluding distressed trust companies.|Q22687|A collective settlement and support institution differs from an individual deposit-taking bank.|

Bretton Woods Conference|topic|named_subject|bretton|Creation of the Bretton Woods System, main account|See how 1944 negotiations combined adjustable exchange-rate commitments with new institutions for payments support and reconstruction.|Q320863|The negotiating event differs from the World Bank Group institution created in its aftermath.|United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference

Bank of England|topic|named_subject|boehistory|1694 foundation; 1946 nationalization entries|Trace the transition from a privately owned government banker to a nationalized central bank.|Q22687|This named institution has a specific ownership and public-finance history distinct from banking generally.|

South Sea Bubble|topic|named_subject|boehistory|1720 South Sea Bubble entry|Examine how national-debt conversion and expectations drove a company's stock boom despite limited trading activity.|Q22687|A specific speculation episode is distinct from a bank or the general concept of financial debt.|

Rochdale Pioneers|topic|named_subject|coopHistory|The Rochdale Pioneers|See how pooling resources, honest retailing, democratic membership, and shared profits formed an influential cooperative model.|Q4539|The named 1844 society differs from the general cooperative form.|Rochdale Equitable Pioneers Society

International Cooperative Alliance|topic|named_subject|coopHistory|Opening 1895 foundation paragraph|Explore how an international federation coordinated information, common principles, and trade among otherwise separate cooperatives.|Q4539|A specific federation is distinct from each member cooperative and from the generic cooperative identity.|ICA

Grameen Bank|topic|named_subject|grameen|About Grameen Bank, pilot and collateral paragraphs|Examine collateral-free village-based lending as an institutional design for reaching borrowers conventional banking may exclude.|Q22687|The named bank's lending model differs from banks generally; selection does not assume all claimed poverty outcomes.|

Toyota Motor Corporation|topic|named_subject|toyota|Production system overview; Jidoka; Just-in-Time|See how the company's production system joins abnormality detection with demand-coordinated flow rather than optimizing only machine speed.|Q167037|A particular corporation's documented production system is distinct from corporations generally.|Toyota

Sakichi Toyoda|topic|named_subject|toyota|Roots of Ideas, How did the idea of Jidoka come about?|Connect his self-stopping loom experiments with the later manufacturing principle of detecting abnormalities at their source.|Q184199|The named inventor and documented loom design lineage differ from the general automation concept.|

Kiichiro Toyoda|topic|named_subject|toyota|Roots of Ideas, How did the idea of Just-in-Time come about?|Explore how limited resources shaped his effort to coordinate automobile parts just when production needed them.|Q187939|The named founder's historical parts-coordination problem differs from manufacturing generally and from the just-in-time method.|
